item.title: Apify
item.description: Apify turns the web into a source of structured data. A marketplace called Apify Store offers thousands of Actors, which are cloud programs that scrape or automate specific websites and tasks: extracting listings from Google Maps, posts from social networks, product details from e-commerce sites, or contact information from pages. You configure an Actor, run it in the cloud, and receive results as JSON, CSV, or through an API, without managing servers or proxies.

item.title: Autodesk Fusion
item.description: Fusion combines the steps of making a physical product in one application. You model parts and assemblies in 3D, run simulations to test stress and heat, and generate toolpaths for CNC machines and 3D printers. It also includes electronics design and drawing tools. Because it runs with cloud-connected data, teams can share designs and collaborate, and it works on both Windows and macOS. Product designers, engineers, machinists, and hobbyists all use it.

item.title: Baserow
item.description:
Baserow gives teams an easy way to build databases. It looks like a spreadsheet, but tables can link to each other, store different field types, and show data as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form. People without coding skills build trackers, inventories, and small internal tools with it.

It is open source, so companies can run it on their own servers, which appeals to those with data residency or privacy needs. The platform has a REST API and webhooks, an application builder for interfaces, and automations that run on triggers. An AI assistant can create tables from a prompt, and AI fields can generate or classify values for each row.

item.title: BigQuery
item.description: BigQuery lets teams analyze huge amounts of data without managing servers. You load data from files, databases, streams, or other Google services, write SQL, and BigQuery spreads the work across many machines and returns results quickly, whether the table holds millions or trillions of rows. Because storage and compute are separated and managed, there is no cluster to size or tune, which is a big reason analytics teams like it.

item.title: Crusoe
item.description:
Crusoe started with a particular idea: use natural gas that would otherwise be burned off at oil wells to power computers. That energy-first approach became a business in cloud computing and then in AI infrastructure, as demand for GPUs rose. Today it builds and operates data centers designed for high-density AI workloads.

Its cloud offers GPU instances, managed Kubernetes and Slurm, and managed inference services for running models, aimed at AI labs and companies that need large amounts of compute. The company emphasizes cleaner energy sources and large campuses for training clusters, working with chip makers and partners to deploy the latest hardware.

item.title: Deepnote
item.description:
Deepnote reimagines the Jupyter notebook for teams. Several people can edit a notebook at once, comment on cells, and run code on managed cloud machines without setup. It connects to data sources such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Postgres, and supports SQL blocks alongside Python, so analysts can mix queries and analysis.

Results are easy to share. Notebooks can be published as interactive apps or dashboards with inputs, charts can be built without code, and scheduled runs keep outputs fresh. Version history and permissions help with team workflows, and it works with common libraries and Jupyter files.

item.title: DISCO
item.description:
DISCO helps legal teams handle the huge volumes of documents produced in lawsuits and investigations. Teams upload email, files, and chats, search and tag them, and decide what is relevant and privileged. The platform runs in the cloud, so reviewers can work together without managing servers.

AI features reduce manual review. Models rank documents by likely relevance, so reviewers see the important ones first, and generative tools summarize documents, answer questions about a set, and help build timelines. Law firms and corporate legal departments use it to cut review costs and speed up cases.

item.title: Dynatrace
item.description:
Dynatrace is one of the established names in monitoring large, complex IT environments. A single agent, OneAgent, installs on servers, containers, and cloud services and automatically discovers applications and their dependencies, then collects metrics, traces, logs, and user experience data without much manual setup. A model of how components relate, kept up to date automatically, lets the platform see how a slowdown in one service affects others.

Its distinguishing feature is Davis AI. Instead of only alerting when thresholds are crossed, Davis uses causal analysis to identify the likely root cause of a problem and the business impact, reducing the pile of alerts into a smaller number of actionable issues. Newer generative AI features let users ask questions in natural language, and the platform adds automation that can trigger remediation. Dynatrace also covers security, application vulnerabilities, and monitoring of AI workloads.

item.title: Filevine
item.description:
Filevine began in personal injury practice and has expanded to many types of law. It gives a firm a single place to track each matter: documents, notes, deadlines, tasks, communications, and billing. Workflows can be customized so that each case type follows the steps a firm wants, with automations that assign tasks and send reminders.

AI features help with the paper-heavy parts of legal work. They can summarize medical records and long case files, draft demand letters and other documents from case data, and help respond to clients. A document review tool extracts key facts and organizes them, which saves paralegals hours on cases with large volumes of material. Client-facing portals and text messaging keep people informed.

item.title: Foxglove
item.description:
Foxglove helps robotics teams understand what their machines did. Robots generate streams from cameras, lidar, GPS, motors, and logs, and debugging requires looking at them together on a timeline. Foxglove’s viewer shows images, point clouds, plots, maps, and 3D scenes in customizable panels that stay synchronized, and it works with ROS and other frameworks.

The platform adds data management. Teams upload recordings to the cloud, search across them by metadata and events, share links to specific moments, and collaborate on issues. The company also created MCAP, an open container format for multimodal robotics data that is now used widely, including as the default recording format in ROS 2.

item.title: Gemini Code Assist
item.description:
Gemini Code Assist brings Google’s models into the developer’s editor. In VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, it suggests code as you type, answers questions in chat, explains and refactors code, generates tests, and helps fix errors. It can take a larger task and make coordinated changes across files in agent mode. Google also offers a command-line version, Gemini CLI, which many developers use directly in the terminal.

For organizations, enterprise editions add code customization, which lets the assistant take into account a company’s private repositories so its suggestions follow internal libraries and styles, as well as security and compliance features, indemnification, and admin controls. It works with Google Cloud tools such as Cloud Shell, Firebase, and BigQuery, and it can review pull requests on GitHub through a companion app.

item.title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech
item.description:
Google Cloud Text-to-Speech gives developers speech synthesis built on the technology behind Google’s assistants. A request with text returns audio in formats like MP3 or WAV, with a choice of voices and languages. The newer voice families, such as WaveNet and the Chirp generation, sound much more natural than traditional synthetic voices, and there are many accents and genders to choose from.

Developers can fine-tune delivery with SSML, adding pauses, emphasis, pronunciation, and speed. The service supports long audio synthesis for audiobooks and narration, and streaming for real-time applications such as voice assistants and interactive voice response systems. Customers can request a custom voice trained on their own recordings, with strict requirements, and the service integrates with other Google Cloud tools.

item.title: Google Cloud Vision
item.description:
Google Cloud Vision is a set of pretrained image analysis features available through an API. Send an image, and it can return labels describing what it contains, detect objects and their locations, read printed and handwritten text, identify landmarks and logos, detect faces and emotions without identifying individuals, and flag explicit content with SafeSearch. It processes single images and batches, including scanned documents.

Typical uses include indexing photo libraries, extracting text from receipts and signs, moderating uploaded images, and powering search by image. Google offers related products for more specialized needs, such as Document AI for forms and Vertex AI for custom models and newer multimodal Gemini models that can describe and reason about images in more detail. Product search features help retailers match photos to catalogs.

item.title: Google Document AI
item.description:
Document AI turns paper and PDF documents into structured data. Prebuilt processors read common document types: invoices with their line items, expense receipts, bank statements, government IDs, and forms. An OCR processor extracts text with layout information, and a layout parser prepares documents for use with language models by splitting them into meaningful chunks.

Customization is a strength. A custom extractor, based on Google’s Gemini models, can be set up with a few examples to pull specific fields from a company’s own documents, even if they vary in layout. A workbench lets teams train and evaluate processors, and a human-in-the-loop option sends uncertain results to reviewers. The output integrates with BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and workflow tools, which helps feed data to analytics and AI systems.

item.title: Grafana
item.description: Grafana is the dashboard tool many engineering teams reach for first. It connects to data sources such as Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, and cloud monitoring services, and lets you build panels and dashboards that visualize time-series data, with alerts that notify teams when something goes wrong. Because it does not store data itself, it can sit on top of whatever you already collect, which is a major reason it is so widely adopted.

item.title: Kaggle
item.description:
Kaggle is where many data scientists learn and prove their skills. Companies and researchers post competitions with real problems, such as predicting outcomes from data or classifying images, and participants submit models to a leaderboard. Winning solutions are often published, and the discussion forums are a rich source of techniques. Rankings and medals help build a public track record.

The platform offers more than contests. Public datasets cover topics from health to sports, free notebooks run Python and R in the browser with access to GPUs and TPUs within limits, and a models hub shares pretrained models. Kaggle Learn provides short, practical courses on Python, pandas, machine learning, and more. Benchmarks and community challenges around large language models have been added, and the site integrates with Google Cloud.

item.title: Magnet Forensics
item.description:
Magnet Forensics serves police, government agencies, and corporate investigators. Its flagship product, Magnet AXIOM, gathers data from devices and online accounts and organizes it so examiners can search messages, photos, browsing history, and app data. Timelines and artifacts help reconstruct what happened and produce reports for legal use.

The company has grown through combination. It merged with Grayshift, which makes tools for accessing locked mobile devices, and offers related products for acquiring evidence, triaging devices at a scene, and reviewing cases collaboratively. AI features help classify images, detect relevant content, and speed up the review of large volumes of data.

item.title: Matillion
item.description:
Matillion is a data integration platform. Data teams use a visual designer to extract data from sources, load it into a cloud warehouse, and transform it there using the warehouse’s own compute. This ELT approach scales with the warehouse and keeps data in the company’s environment.

AI has become part of the product through Maia, a set of agents that act as virtual data engineers. A user describes what they need, and Maia can create pipelines, suggest fixes when something fails, and write documentation. Humans stay in the loop and can review the generated work. The platform also supports orchestration, scheduling, and version control with Git.

item.title: Mentimeter
item.description:
Mentimeter makes presentations interactive. You build slides with questions such as multiple choice polls, word clouds, rating scales, rankings, and open-ended questions, share a join code or QR code, and the audience responds from their phones. Results appear live on the screen, which turns a one-way talk into a conversation and gives quiet participants an easy way to contribute.

It suits a range of settings. Teachers use it to check understanding, trainers to energize workshops, and companies to run all-hands meetings and collect anonymous feedback. Features include quizzes with leaderboards, Q&A with upvoting, and templates, and you can import existing slides from PowerPoint or Google Slides. AI helps generate a presentation from a prompt, suggest questions, and summarize responses.

item.title: Oracle NetSuite
item.description:
NetSuite was one of the first cloud ERP systems and is widely used by growing companies. A single system runs financials, inventory, procurement, order management, billing, and customer relationship management, so departments work from the same data instead of reconciling spreadsheets. Industry editions adapt it for areas like wholesale distribution, manufacturing, retail, and software, and it supports multiple subsidiaries, currencies, and tax rules, which suits companies expanding internationally.

AI features sit across the suite. Generative tools can summarize records, draft emails and descriptions, and answer questions about data in plain language, while machine learning supports forecasting, anomaly detection, and automation of accounting tasks like matching invoices. Reporting and analytics tools let finance teams build dashboards, and SuiteScript and workflows allow customization.

item.title: Pendo
item.description:
Pendo helps product teams understand and improve their software. After adding a snippet to an application, Pendo records usage automatically: which pages and features people use, where they drop off, and how behavior varies by customer or segment. Product managers use dashboards, funnels, and retention reports to decide what to build and what to fix.

The platform lets teams act on insights without waiting for developers. In-app guides, tooltips, announcements, and checklists guide users through features, surveys and NPS collect feedback, and a roadmap tool captures feature requests. Session replay shows what people did, and AI features summarize feedback, suggest improvements, and analyze conversations with AI features inside products, which is a growing need as software adds assistants.

item.title: Qualio
item.description:
Qualio is designed for regulated life sciences companies that need a quality system but not a heavy enterprise one. Teams write and approve controlled documents, assign and track training, manage change requests and corrective actions, and keep the records auditors expect, all in a cloud app with electronic signatures.

The product is aimed at smaller and growth-stage companies. Pre-built templates and workflows speed up setup, and the platform adds modules for events, risk, and supplier qualification. AI features help draft and review documents and answer questions about the quality system.

item.title: Secureframe
item.description:
Secureframe automates compliance work. It integrates with cloud providers, code repositories, identity systems, and HR tools to check that required controls are in place, gather evidence for auditors, and alert teams when something drifts out of compliance.

The platform also manages policies, employee training, vendor risk, and a trust page for customers. AI drafts policies, maps controls across frameworks, and fills in security questionnaires from a company’s own answers, saving time during sales cycles.

item.title: SentinelOne
item.description:
SentinelOne is a cybersecurity company known for autonomous endpoint protection. Its agent runs on computers and servers, uses machine learning to detect malicious behavior on the device, and can respond automatically by isolating a machine, killing a process, or rolling back changes made by ransomware. That local decision-making works even when a device is offline.

The Singularity platform extends this across the environment. It brings together endpoint detection and response with cloud workload security, identity threat detection, vulnerability management, and a data lake that collects logs from many sources for threat hunting. Purple AI is a generative assistant that lets analysts ask questions in natural language, such as whether a suspicious file appeared elsewhere, and turns them into queries, summarizes findings, and suggests next steps.

item.title: Veeva Systems
item.description:
Veeva is the dominant software vendor for pharmaceutical companies. Its CRM supports sales and medical teams that engage with physicians, Vault is a cloud platform for managing documents and processes in areas such as clinical operations, regulatory submissions, quality, and safety, and data products supply information about healthcare providers and markets. Companies use these tools to run regulated, document-heavy processes.

The company has been adding AI across its applications. Veeva AI agents help users search content, prepare documents, and automate steps such as drafting summaries or checking submissions, built into Vault and its CRM and operating under the industry’s compliance requirements. It has also moved its CRM off the Salesforce platform onto its own technology.

item.title: Xero
item.description:
Xero is an online accounting platform used widely in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, and increasingly elsewhere. Business owners and bookkeepers connect their bank accounts so transactions flow in automatically, then match them to invoices and bills in a reconciliation process that Xero makes quick with suggested matches. It generates invoices, tracks expenses and cash flow, and produces reports such as profit and loss and balance sheets.

An accountant-friendly design is part of its appeal. Unlimited users on most plans let owners, bookkeepers, and accountants work in the same file, and a large marketplace of integrations connects Xero to payment providers, payroll, inventory, and point-of-sale systems. AI features include suggested coding of transactions, predictive cash flow tools, and an assistant for asking questions about the business and automating tasks like drafting invoice reminders.

item.title: CAST AI
item.description:
CAST AI is an automation layer for Kubernetes. After connecting to a cluster on AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure, it analyzes workloads, chooses the best-priced instance types, scales nodes up and down, and replaces expensive capacity with spot instances when workloads can tolerate interruptions.

The platform also covers related needs. Savings reports show the effect, workload autoscaling adjusts resource requests, and security scanning finds misconfigurations. More recently it added tools for running GPU workloads and AI inference more efficiently. Customers keep their own cloud accounts.

item.title: DocumentCloud
item.description:
DocumentCloud is a platform built for newsrooms. Reporters upload documents such as court filings, government reports, and leaked files, and the system makes them searchable through optical character recognition. They can annotate passages, add notes, and publish documents so readers can see the original source behind a story.

For large collections, the tool helps with analysis. Entity extraction finds people, places, and organizations mentioned, and search across projects lets teams collaborate on investigations. Add-ons extend the system with automated tasks, including redaction, translation, and data extraction.

item.title: Everlaw
item.description:
Everlaw helps legal teams work through evidence. Documents are uploaded, processed, and made searchable, and reviewers tag them, share notes, and build case narratives. Visual tools show relationships and timelines, and cloud delivery means teams can collaborate without installing software.

AI speeds up the work. Predictive coding ranks documents by likely relevance, clustering groups similar content, and generative features summarize documents, answer questions across a set, and draft deposition outlines. Everlaw has tools used by public interest lawyers and human rights investigators, and the company supports access programs.

item.title: Kentik
item.description:
Kentik gives network teams insight into how traffic moves. It collects flow records, routing information, and metrics from routers, switches, and cloud networks, stores them at large scale, and lets engineers query who is talking to whom and how much. That helps with capacity planning, troubleshooting, and cost control.

Security and reliability uses include detecting DDoS attacks and unusual traffic patterns, analyzing BGP routing changes, and finding the reason for a slowdown across multiple networks. An AI assistant lets users ask questions in plain language and speeds up root cause analysis. Cloud and data center networks are covered.

item.title: Grok Bot
item.description:
Grok Bot takes a different shape from a chat window. A user creates named bots and assigns them tasks, and each bot runs in the cloud, keeps working after the user closes their laptop, and can sign into apps and use a browser to complete work. Examples include handling inbox tasks, researching topics, and running routine workflows.

The product emphasizes persistence. Bots remember context over time and report back, and the cloud computer gives them a place to store files and run tools. It is positioned for both individuals and businesses, with a business version aimed at agents that log into company applications.

item.title: OpenAI Daybreak
item.description:
Daybreak gives defenders access to frontier AI for security work. Approved organizations use models for tasks such as triaging incidents, analyzing malware, validating patches, and hunting for vulnerabilities, with workflows designed for security teams.

OpenAI split access into tiers. A defender tier provides frontier models without some of the safeguards that might block legitimate security prompts, and a more specialized tier provides models trained for higher-risk testing such as vulnerability research and exploit validation. Access is limited to vetted individuals and organizations.

item.title: Cloudflare Kitesurf
item.description:
Kitesurf rethinks the browser for software. Most automation tools control a full desktop browser, which is heavy and built around human use. Kitesurf is a lean browser written to run inside Cloudflare’s Workers platform, so an agent can open pages, read them, and click or type without the overhead of a complete Chrome instance.

It works with existing tools. Clients that use Puppeteer, Playwright, or the Model Context Protocol can connect to it through Cloudflare’s browser service with small changes. The design treats every page as untrusted and starts each session fresh, which suits agent security. Cloudflare says it uses less memory than Chromium in its tests.

item.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway
item.description:
AI Gateway is a proxy for calls to language models. A developer points their app’s requests at a Cloudflare URL instead of the provider’s, and the gateway forwards them while recording what happens. This gives a dashboard of requests, tokens, costs, and errors across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

It adds control features. Caching returns stored answers for repeated requests to save money and time, rate limits protect budgets, and retries and fallbacks switch to another model when one fails. Logging helps debug prompts, and guardrails and key management features support security.

item.title: NVIDIA NIM
item.description:
NIM, short for NVIDIA Inference Microservices, packages a model so it is easy to deploy. Each microservice includes the model, optimized inference engines such as TensorRT-LLM, and standard APIs, delivered as a container. A team can run it on a cloud, a data center, or a workstation with NVIDIA GPUs and get tuned performance.

A catalog covers language models, vision, speech, and biology models from NVIDIA and partners, with APIs compatible with common formats such as OpenAI’s. Enterprises use NIM to keep models and data inside their environment while reaching production speed.

item.title: OpenVINO
item.description:
OpenVINO helps run models efficiently on Intel hardware. A developer takes a model from PyTorch, TensorFlow, or ONNX, converts it, and optimizes it with techniques like quantization, then runs it on CPUs, integrated and discrete GPUs, and neural processing units. This makes AI practical on laptops and edge devices without a high-end graphics card.

Newer parts target generative AI, including support for language models and image generation, with a GenAI library and integration with Hugging Face. Model servers and tools support deployment in applications.

item.title: Qualcomm AI Hub
item.description:
Qualcomm AI Hub targets on-device AI for phones, PCs, and other products built with Qualcomm chips. A developer uploads a model, and the service converts and optimizes it for the target hardware, then runs it on real devices in the cloud to measure speed and accuracy.

A library of ready-to-run models, such as vision, speech, and language models, saves time. Profiling shows where a model spends time and memory, guiding further tuning. The goal is to make it easy to run AI locally, with benefits for privacy, cost, and latency.

item.title: Tencent Cloud ADP
item.description:
Tencent Cloud ADP gives companies tools to create agents. Users connect knowledge bases for retrieval, design workflows with a visual editor, and combine agents that work together. Models include Tencent’s Hunyuan family and others.

Typical applications are customer service, internal assistants, and process automation. The platform includes tools for testing and monitoring and integrates with Tencent’s ecosystem, including WeChat and enterprise messaging.

It is sold on usage-based pricing within Tencent Cloud. Outside China, availability and support are more limited, and organizations must consider data residency. Alternatives include Alibaba Cloud’s Bailian, Baidu Qianfan, ByteDance’s Volcano Engine, Dify, and AWS Bedrock Agents. Tencent Cloud ADP suits companies building agents on Tencent Cloud.

item.title: Born to Found
item.description:
Born to Found guides first-time founders through the early journey. It divides company building into stages, such as validating an idea, building a first product, and finding customers, and supplies playbooks and checklists for each, so a founder knows what to focus on at their point.

An AI coach answers questions and reviews work, drawing on the founder’s stage and project details. This offers a low-cost alternative to mentors for people who lack access to experienced advisors, and a structure to keep going when the path is unclear.

item.title: BentoML
item.description:
BentoML tackles the step between a working model and a running service. A developer writes a small Python service that loads a model, defines an API, and handles requests. BentoML builds this into a standard package, called a Bento, that includes dependencies and can be turned into a Docker container.

The framework supports features that production services need: batching requests for efficiency, running multiple models, GPU use, and monitoring. It works with models from PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, Hugging Face, and others, and supports large language model serving through optimized backends. BentoCloud is the company’s managed platform for deploying and scaling.

item.title: Databricks
item.description:
Databricks started with Apache Spark and grew into a unified platform for data work. Companies store data in open formats in their cloud, then use Databricks for pipelines, SQL analytics, notebooks, and machine learning, with a governance layer called Unity Catalog that controls access and tracks lineage across it all.

AI has become central to the pitch. The platform supports training and fine-tuning models, serving them through endpoints, vector search for retrieval, and a framework for building agents grounded in enterprise data. The company acquired MosaicML to strengthen model training, and offers tools to monitor and evaluate AI systems. An assistant helps write code and queries.

item.title: MLflow
item.description:
MLflow began at Databricks as a way to bring order to machine learning work. Teams log parameters, metrics, code versions, and artifacts for each run, compare results in a web interface, and package models in a standard format that can be deployed in many environments. A model registry manages versions and stages.

The project has extended to generative AI. It supports tracing of LLM applications, evaluation tools, and prompt management, making it useful for teams building with language models as well as classic models. It works with most ML libraries and cloud platforms.

item.title: MotherDuck
item.description:
MotherDuck takes the DuckDB analytical database, which runs on a laptop, and adds a cloud service. A user connects from their local DuckDB, queries data in the cloud, and combines it with local files, in what the company calls hybrid execution, using each machine for what it does best.

It targets teams that do not need a large data warehouse. Features include shared databases, collaboration, integrations with common data tools, and an AI assistant that helps write SQL. The pitch is simple, fast analytics at lower cost for data in the gigabytes to terabytes range.

item.title: Render
item.description:
Render simplifies hosting. A developer connects a repository, and Render builds and runs the app, handles TLS certificates, and scales as needed. It supports web services, static sites, cron jobs, private services, and managed Postgres and Redis.

Preview environments build each pull request automatically, and infrastructure can be defined in a file. Teams like its predictable pricing and straightforward interface, and it works for AI apps that need background workers and databases.

item.title: Snowflake
item.description:
Snowflake pioneered the cloud data warehouse built on this separation. Companies load data, run SQL queries with elastic compute, and share datasets securely with partners. It runs on the major clouds, and teams of analysts and engineers use it as a central data foundation.

The platform has grown into an AI data cloud. Cortex provides language model functions, search over documents, and agents that run inside the platform, close to the data, with governance. It also supports machine learning, Python workloads, and apps built on Snowflake data.

item.title: SYSTRAN
item.description:
SYSTRAN is among the oldest names in machine translation. Its modern products use neural models, offered as an API, a desktop app, and server software that can run inside an organization’s own network. This matters for sensitive documents.

Customization lets organizations tune translation to their terminology, and the platform handles many file formats and language pairs. Government and corporate customers use it for large volumes of content.

SYSTRAN is sold by subscription and license. General-purpose language models now compete in translation quality. Alternatives include DeepL, Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, Amazon Translate, and Lilt. SYSTRAN suits organizations needing private, deployable translation.

item.title: Transifex
item.description:
Transifex helps product teams translate content into many languages. Developers connect repositories such as GitHub and GitLab, or use a command-line tool, and new text is sent to Transifex for translation. Translators and reviewers work in an online editor with translation memory, glossaries, and context, and approved translations flow back to the codebase.

A distinctive piece is Transifex Native, which lets apps fetch translations through an SDK, so updating a translation doesn’t require a new release. AI and machine translation pre-translate content, and quality checks flag issues, while workflows route text through reviewers or professional translation vendors. Integrations cover design tools, content management systems, and help centers.

item.title: Turso
item.description:
Turso brings SQLite to the cloud. libSQL adds features to SQLite such as network access and replication, and Turso hosts databases and replicates them to regions near users for fast reads. It also supports embedded replicas that live inside an application.

The model suits products with a database per user or tenant, because creating a new database is cheap. Vector search support helps with AI features, and agents can use databases as disposable storage.

item.title: Zilliz
item.description:
Zilliz Cloud runs Milvus as a service. Teams avoid operating clusters themselves and get a managed database for embeddings with features such as automatic scaling, backups, and security controls. It supports search for recommendations, retrieval for AI applications, and image or audio similarity.

Zilliz created Milvus and contributes to the open-source project, which means customers can move between self-hosting and the managed service. Hybrid search, filtering, and multi-tenant setups serve production workloads.

item.title: Looker
item.description:
Looker takes a modeling-first approach. Data teams define dimensions and measures in LookML, a code-based language, and users explore data and build dashboards on top of those shared definitions. This keeps numbers consistent and cuts arguments over whose revenue figure is right.

The platform queries data warehouses directly, so it works with the company’s data without extracting it. It supports embedded analytics, letting companies put dashboards in their own products. Gemini in Looker adds conversational analytics and help writing LookML and building reports.

item.title: Pix4D
item.description:
Pix4D is photogrammetry software. Photos taken by a drone or a camera are processed into orthomosaics, digital surface models, and 3D meshes with accurate coordinates, so users can measure distances, areas, and volumes from the results.

Products target different jobs. One handles mapping from drones, another focuses on surveying with scanners and phones, and others serve fields like agriculture and inspection. AI helps classify features and clean up point clouds, and cloud processing handles big projects.

item.title: FARO
item.description:
FARO’s scanners measure a space by sweeping a laser and recording millions of points, which form a detailed 3D copy of a room, a crash site, or a factory. Software then turns the point cloud into measurements, floor plans, and models. The captured scene can be revisited long after a site has been cleaned up.

Forensic and public safety teams use it to document crime and crash scenes and to reconstruct events. Architecture, engineering, and construction firms scan buildings to check progress against designs and to capture existing conditions. Manufacturing uses related tools for inspection and measurement of parts.

item.title: Adobe Character Animator
item.description:
Character Animator brings puppets to life. You prepare a character in Photoshop or Illustrator with layers for eyes, mouth, and body parts, import it, and the software maps your face and voice to the character. As you speak and move, the character blinks, talks, and reacts in real time, with lip sync generated from your audio.

It was designed for speed. Rigged characters can be recorded live, and the performance can be edited afterward on a timeline. Triggers set up with keyboard keys can switch poses, props, or expressions. The tool has been used for animated shows, live broadcasts, and explainer videos, and it integrates with Premiere Pro and After Effects.

item.title: ArcGIS
item.description: ArcGIS is the leading commercial GIS platform. Governments, utilities, environmental agencies, city planners, and businesses use it to collect location data, display it on maps, and analyze spatial relationships, such as which neighborhoods lie within a flood zone or where to place a new store. The product family includes ArcGIS Pro for desktop analysis, ArcGIS Online as a cloud service for building and sharing maps, and ArcGIS Enterprise for organizations that run their own servers.

item.title: Arterys
item.description:
Arterys was an early company in medical imaging AI. Its cloud platform ran deep-learning tools on scans such as cardiac MRI, chest CT, and liver studies, helping radiologists and cardiologists measure and analyze images faster. It was among the first companies to receive regulatory clearance in the United States for a deep-learning clinical application, and its viewer was designed to be used inside the browser without special workstations.

The platform’s main idea was to embed AI directly in the workflow clinicians already use. It connected to hospital systems such as PACS and electronic health records, so results appeared alongside the images instead of in a separate tool. Automating routine measurements, like heart chamber volumes, could save time and reduce variation between readers.

item.title: Autodesk Construction Cloud
item.description:
Autodesk Construction Cloud brings together the tools that general contractors, owners, and subcontractors use to run building projects. A shared data environment keeps drawings, models, and documents in one place with version control, so everyone works from the current set. Teams use it for design review, model coordination across disciplines, quantity takeoff, cost estimating, issue tracking, and quality and safety checks in the field.

Autodesk has been folding the product line into Forma, its industry cloud, and the construction products now carry the Forma name, such as Forma Build, Forma Data Management, Forma Takeoff, and Forma Estimate. They connect to Autodesk’s design tools like Revit, which keeps information flowing from the design model to the construction site. AI features help automate routine work and surface insights, for example by flagging risks, extracting information from documents, or speeding up takeoff.

item.title: Avalara
item.description: Avalara helps businesses get indirect taxes right. Sales tax rules vary by state, city, product type, and customer, and rates change often, which makes manual calculation risky. Avalara integrates with online stores, accounting software, and ERP systems to calculate the correct tax at checkout or invoicing based on the transaction’s location and product, then helps file returns and remit payments in many jurisdictions. It covers sales and use tax, VAT, and other transaction taxes around the world.

item.title: AWS IoT Core
item.description:
AWS IoT Core is the entry point for Internet of Things devices into AWS. Devices connect using MQTT, HTTPS, and other protocols, authenticate with certificates, and publish and receive messages, with the service scaling to billions of devices and trillions of messages. A device registry tracks each device, and Device Shadows keep a copy of the device’s state so applications can interact with it even when it is offline.

A rules engine processes incoming data and routes it to other AWS services such as Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, Kinesis, and SageMaker, so data can be stored, analyzed, or used to trigger actions. Related services handle device management, fleet monitoring, over-the-air updates, and edge computing with AWS IoT Greengrass, which runs code and machine learning models on the device. Security features include fine-grained policies, and logging and monitoring tools.

item.title: AWS Rekognition
item.description: Rekognition lets developers add image and video analysis to an application without training a model from scratch. You send an image or a video and get back detected objects and scenes, text found in the picture, faces with attributes such as glasses or smiling, and flags for unsafe or inappropriate content. It works on photos, stored video files, and live video streams, and it integrates with S3, Lambda, and other AWS services.

item.title: Azure IoT Hub
item.description: Azure IoT Hub is the messaging backbone for connected devices on Azure. Devices send telemetry such as sensor readings to the cloud, and the cloud can send commands and configuration back. Each device has its own identity and credentials, so the platform can authenticate it, and connections use standard protocols like MQTT and AMQP. The hub scales to large fleets and can route messages to storage, stream processing, and analytics services.

item.title: Bambu Studio
item.description:
Bambu Studio turns 3D model files into instructions a printer can follow. You load a model, arrange it on the virtual build plate, set options such as layer height, supports, and infill, and the slicer generates the toolpath, previewing how the print will be built. It supports multicolor and multimaterial printing through Bambu’s automatic material system, with tools to assign colors and manage waste.

It is based on open-source slicer code and is itself open source. Features include automatic calibration, print profiles tuned for Bambu printers and common filaments, remote monitoring and control over the cloud, and integration with MakerWorld, Bambu’s online library of models, where users share designs and print profiles. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux and also supports some other printers.

item.title: Benchling
item.description: Benchling brings the scattered tasks of a research lab into one cloud system. Scientists use the notebook to record experiments, design DNA and protein sequences with molecular biology tools, and register the samples and materials they create, so everything is traceable. Teams track workflows, share results, and connect lab instruments, which replaces a mix of spreadsheets, paper notebooks, and separate databases. It is common at startups and large biopharma companies.

item.title: BigID
item.description:
BigID starts with a question many companies cannot answer: where is our sensitive data? It scans databases, file shares, cloud storage, SaaS apps, and data lakes to discover personal information, financial records, and other regulated data, then classifies it using machine learning. The results build a catalog showing what data exists, where it sits, and who can access it. That map is the basis for privacy and security work.

Several functions build on the catalog. Privacy teams use it to respond to access and deletion requests, track consent, and meet rules like GDPR and CCPA. Security teams use it to find overexposed data, fix permissions, and reduce risk through remediation workflows. A newer focus is AI governance: the platform identifies which AI agents, copilots, and models can reach sensitive data, helps limit that access, and checks against frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act.

item.title: CloudHealth by VMware
item.description: CloudHealth was one of the first tools built for managing cloud costs across several providers. Companies connect their AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts and get a consolidated view of spending, broken down by team, project, or application using tags and rules. Reports show where money goes, budgets raise alerts when spending drifts, and recommendations point to unused resources and oversized instances. That helps finance and engineering teams share a view of cloud costs.

item.title: CrowdStrike
item.description: CrowdStrike’s core product is Falcon, a cloud-based endpoint security platform. A small agent on laptops, servers, and cloud workloads sends behavior data to CrowdStrike’s cloud, where machine learning and threat intelligence look for malicious activity such as ransomware or hands-on-keyboard attacks. Because analysis happens in the cloud, the agent is light and updates quickly. The company’s detection and response model, known as EDR and XDR, is widely used by large enterprises and governments.

item.title: Datadog
item.description: Datadog is software-as-a-service for watching what your systems are doing. You install an agent on servers, containers, or cloud accounts, or connect it through one of hundreds of integrations, and it begins collecting metrics, logs, and traces. Dashboards and alerts then show how hosts, databases, queues, and services are behaving. The value for most teams is having infrastructure monitoring, application performance monitoring, log management, and real user monitoring in one place instead of stitching together separate tools.

item.title: DNAnexus
item.description: DNAnexus gives life science organizations a place to work with very large datasets. Sequencing a genome produces enormous files, and analyzing thousands of them takes substantial computing and careful data management. The platform provides cloud storage, scalable compute, workflow tools, and a catalog of bioinformatics pipelines, so teams can run analyses without managing their own servers. It is built to meet regulatory and privacy requirements for clinical and health data.

item.title: Fauna
item.description:
Fauna set out to give developers a database that scaled globally without managing servers. It combined a flexible document model with relational features, offered strong consistency across regions, and was accessed through an API with its own query language, FQL, and earlier through GraphQL. Developers built web and mobile apps on it without running infrastructure.

The company announced that it would wind down its hosted service, and the service closed, with accounts deleted afterward. It also said it would release parts of its technology as open source, so some of the ideas may live on in community projects.

item.title: Formant
item.description:
Formant solves operational problems that arise once robots leave the lab. Companies running fleets of mobile robots, drones, or arms need to know what each machine is doing, diagnose problems, and sometimes take control. Formant collects telemetry, video, and sensor data from robots, shows it in dashboards, and raises alerts when something goes wrong, working with robots running ROS or other software.

Teleoperation is a key feature: an operator can view a robot’s cameras and drive or guide it remotely, which helps with situations where autonomy fails. Teams can capture and tag data to improve machine learning models, schedule and analyze missions, and manage software updates across a fleet. Integrations connect with cloud services and business systems, and AI tools help find anomalies.

item.title: Particle
item.description:
Particle gives hardware teams a full stack for connected devices. It sells development boards and production-ready modules with cellular, Wi-Fi, or Bluetooth connectivity, runs its own device operating system, and provides a cloud console to monitor devices, send commands, and update firmware over the air. Because connectivity, SIM management, and cloud services come bundled, a small team can move from prototype to production without assembling the parts separately.

The platform emphasizes fleet management at scale. Dashboards show device health and data usage, alerts flag problems, and tools support provisioning, remote diagnostics, and secure updates. Webhooks and integrations send data to cloud services and applications, and newer products add more powerful edge computing, including boards that run Android and machine learning workloads at the edge.

item.title: Rookout
item.description:
Rookout solved a frustrating problem: figuring out what is happening inside production code. Normally, finding a bug means adding logging, redeploying, and waiting for the problem to recur. Rookout let developers set non-breaking breakpoints in live applications, so they could capture variable values, stack traces, and logs on demand without stopping the program or changing and restarting it.

It supported cloud-native environments with containers, serverless functions, and Kubernetes, and integrated with the tools developers already used for logging and monitoring. The data could be sent to existing observability systems, so debugging fit into current workflows. It was used by engineering teams that needed to debug complex, distributed applications quickly.

item.title: Samsara
item.description:
Samsara collects data from the physical world and puts it to work. Gateways and cameras installed on vehicles, trailers, and equipment report location, engine data, driver behavior, and conditions, and the cloud platform presents it through dashboards and apps. Fleet managers use it for tracking, routing, maintenance, compliance with driver hours rules, and safety coaching.

AI dashcams detect risky events like distracted driving, tailgating, and rolling stops, and alert drivers and managers, and video evidence helps with accidents and insurance claims. The platform also covers equipment monitoring, site safety, temperature tracking for cold chains, and workflow tools such as digital forms and inspections. An AI assistant helps users analyze data and set up actions in plain language.

item.title: Spire Global
item.description:
Spire builds and operates a large fleet of small satellites known as nanosatellites. Instead of taking photographs, they listen: they pick up radio signals from ships, aircraft, and GPS signals bouncing off the Earth, and measure atmospheric conditions. The resulting data feeds products that track vessels around the world, monitor air traffic, and improve weather forecasts.

The business sells data and analytics as a service. Maritime customers use it to follow ships, estimate arrival times, and detect suspicious behavior, aviation customers use it for flight tracking, and meteorological agencies use radio occultation data to enhance forecasts. Spire also provides space services, building and operating satellites for customers. Machine learning supports forecasting and anomaly detection in the data, and APIs deliver it to customers’ systems.

item.title: Spot.io
item.description:
Spot started as Spotinst, a company that helped users run workloads on cheap but interruptible cloud capacity. Its Elastigroup service predicts when spot instances will be reclaimed and moves workloads to keep applications running, which can reduce compute costs sharply. Ocean applies the same ideas to Kubernetes clusters, scaling nodes and choosing instance types automatically, and Eco manages savings plans and reserved instances.

NetApp acquired Spot, branded it Spot by NetApp, and later sold the Spot FinOps portfolio to Flexera, which now develops it alongside its other cloud cost tools. The tools support AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, with dashboards showing savings, and they are sold on a model tied to a percentage of savings or capacity. Customers have included engineering teams running large container and batch workloads.

item.title: Transcend
item.description:
Transcend takes a developer-oriented approach to privacy compliance. It connects to a company’s databases, SaaS tools, and warehouses to discover where personal data is stored, then automates responses to requests from individuals to access or delete their data. Instead of manually searching dozens of systems, the platform executes the request across them and keeps a record.

Other products cover related needs. Consent management controls cookies and tracking according to each visitor’s choices and location, a gateway can enforce those choices in what data flows to third parties, and data mapping documents processing activities. Newer tools address AI governance, helping teams track what data feeds models and meet emerging regulations.

item.title: Turbonomic
item.description: Turbonomic tries to answer a question that infrastructure teams face constantly: is each application getting the resources it needs without wasting money? The platform monitors applications and the infrastructure they run on, including virtual machines, containers, and cloud services, and uses analytics to decide where workloads should run, how large they should be, and when to scale. It can take actions automatically, such as resizing instances, moving workloads, or adjusting Kubernetes resources.

item.title: Vanta
item.description:
Vanta helps companies prove they run secure operations. It integrates with tools such as AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, Okta, and HR systems, continuously checks whether controls like encryption, access reviews, and employee training are in place, and collects the evidence auditors need. This replaces manual screenshots and spreadsheets and keeps a company audit-ready year-round.

The platform has grown into a broader trust management suite. It tracks vendor risk, manages security policies and employee onboarding tasks, runs risk assessments, and provides a trust center where customers can see a company’s security posture. AI features answer security questionnaires, map controls across frameworks, and help prioritize remediation, saving time for small security teams.

item.title: Wiz
item.description: Wiz became one of the fastest-growing security companies by making cloud risk easier to see. It connects to cloud accounts through APIs and snapshots, without installing agents on every machine, and builds a graph of resources, identities, networks, and data. From that graph it finds problems such as exposed storage, over-permissive roles, unpatched software, and secrets in code, and it shows how they could be chained together into an attack path to something valuable.

item.title: Adobe Firefly
item.description: Firefly is Adobe’s generative AI platform. The Firefly web app generates images from a text description, extends or edits existing ones, creates short video clips, and produces audio and vector artwork. Adobe trained its own models on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it markets them as safer for commercial use than models trained on scraped images. Outputs carry content credentials that note they were made with AI.

item.title: Amazon CodeWhisperer
item.description:
CodeWhisperer was Amazon’s first coding assistant, a counterpart to GitHub Copilot that suggested lines and whole functions as you typed in editors such as VS Code and the JetBrains IDEs. It was trained with a special focus on AWS APIs, so it was particularly good at code that called S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, and other AWS services. It also supported many popular programming languages.

Two features set it apart from early rivals. A reference tracker flagged suggestions that resembled open-source code and showed the license, and a security scan checked your code for vulnerabilities such as exposed credentials and injection flaws. An individual tier was free, and a professional tier added admin controls and higher limits.

item.title: AnythingLLM
item.description:
AnythingLLM gives you a private place to talk to your files. You add documents, web pages, or other content to a workspace, and the app indexes them in a vector database. When you ask a question, it retrieves relevant passages and sends them to a language model, which answers with references.

Flexibility is the main draw. You can choose a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, or a cloud model from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and swap them without rebuilding your workspace. It has agents that can browse the web or run tools, supports multiple users and permissions in the server version, and offers an API and embeddable chat widget.

item.title: Anytype
item.description:
Anytype is a workspace for notes and structured information built around privacy. Data is stored locally and encrypted, and syncs between devices peer to peer or through backup nodes, so you keep ownership of your content rather than leaving it on a company server. The app is open source.

Its model uses objects and types. Everything is an object, such as a page, a person, a book, or a task, and each type has fields. Objects link to each other and appear in sets and collections, which function like databases. This lets users create a personal wiki or a custom organizer without code. Optional AI features can summarize and help write.

item.title: AWS GovCloud
item.description: AWS GovCloud is a separate set of AWS regions built for workloads that carry strict regulatory requirements. US government agencies, contractors, and other organizations handling controlled data use it to host systems that must comply with standards such as FedRAMP High, the Department of Defense Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide, ITAR, CJIS, and HIPAA. The regions are physically and logically isolated from the standard AWS regions, and access is restricted to vetted US citizens.

item.title: BambooHR
item.description:
BambooHR is built for companies without a large HR department. It keeps employee information in one place, tracks time off, handles onboarding checklists and documents, and offers an employee self-service portal. Applicant tracking helps with hiring, performance tools support reviews and goals, and payroll and benefits administration are available for U.S. customers. Reporting shows headcount, turnover, and other metrics.

The product is known for being easy to use, with a friendly interface and quick setup. AI features help HR teams with tasks such as drafting job descriptions and performance review language, summarizing feedback, and answering employee questions using company policies. Integrations connect with accounting, benefits, and productivity tools, and an app marketplace extends the platform.

item.title: Bubble
item.description:
Bubble lets people build real web apps without programming. The editor works by placing elements on a page, defining a database, and setting up workflows that say what happens when a user clicks or a condition occurs. Apps can include logins, payments, and integrations with other services.

It is used for marketplaces, internal tools, SaaS products, and prototypes, and some companies run substantial businesses on it. AI features can generate a starting app or page layout from a description, and plugins extend functionality. Bubble hosts the app, so there is no server to manage.

item.title: Bubble
item.description: Bubble lets people build real software without writing code. You design pages by dragging elements onto a canvas, define what happens when users click or submit with visual workflows, and store data in a built-in database. That is enough to build marketplaces, internal tools, customer portals, and SaaS products. Because the logic is visual but still detailed, Bubble apps can be quite complex, which is why it has been popular with founders who want to test an idea before hiring developers.

item.title: Chatbase
item.description: Chatbase started as a simple way to create a chatbot from your own data. You upload files, point it to a website, or connect sources such as Notion, and it builds an agent that answers questions using that information. You embed the chat widget on your site with a snippet of code and you have support available around the clock. The simplicity made it popular with small businesses and startups that wanted a support bot without engineering work.

item.title: Civitai
item.description:
Civitai is where much of the open-source image generation community meets. Creators upload checkpoints, LoRAs, embeddings, and other add-ons for Stable Diffusion, FLUX, and related models, together with sample images and the prompts used. Others download them to run locally in tools like ComfyUI or Automatic1111, or try them in the browser. Ratings, comments, and example galleries make it easier to judge a model before downloading.

The site offers more than a library. Users can generate images on Civitai’s servers using credits, train their own LoRAs from a set of images, and take part in challenges and bounties that reward creators. Articles and guides share techniques, and a point system pays for the use of the site’s services. It became the unofficial catalog for community-trained styles, characters, and concepts.

item.title: CoreWeave
item.description:
CoreWeave began as a company mining cryptocurrency and turned its GPU capacity into a cloud for AI. Customers rent clusters of NVIDIA GPUs for training and running models, with networking and storage built for large workloads. Because it specializes, it can often deploy new GPU generations quickly.

The platform runs on Kubernetes and offers managed services for training, inference, and storage. Major AI labs and big technology companies have signed large contracts, and the company has built or leased data centers around the world. It acquired Weights & Biases to add developer tooling to its infrastructure.

item.title: dbt Cloud
item.description:
dbt, short for data build tool, became the standard way to transform raw data inside a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Analysts write SQL select statements, define dependencies among them, and dbt builds tables and views in the right order, with version control, testing, and documentation. This brings software engineering practices like code review and continuous integration to analytics work.

dbt Cloud is the hosted product from dbt Labs. It provides a browser-based IDE, job scheduling, CI that tests changes before they reach production, a data catalog with lineage, and a semantic layer that defines metrics once for use across BI tools. AI features help generate models, tests, and documentation, and answer questions about the project, which speeds up repetitive tasks.

item.title: Dolby.io
item.description:
Dolby.io brings Dolby’s audio expertise to developers as web services. A developer sends an audio or video file and receives a processed version: cleaner speech, reduced background noise, balanced loudness, or improved dialogue. These APIs fit podcast tools, video platforms, and conferencing products.

Other parts of the platform focus on real-time streaming. Millicast delivers low-latency video to large audiences, which suits live events, interactive broadcasts, and remote production. Analysis and transcoding APIs help prepare content for different devices.

item.title: Domo AI
item.description:
Domo aims to put an organization’s data in one place. It connects to hundreds of sources, from databases and spreadsheets to marketing and finance platforms, and lets users clean and combine data and then build dashboards and reports. Business users can view metrics on the web or mobile and set alerts, and developers can build custom apps on top of the data.

AI is built through the product. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive charts and answers, models can forecast and detect anomalies, and AI agents and workflows can automate tasks, such as summarizing reports or triggering actions when numbers change. Domo also lets companies connect their own models, and offers governance features for data access.

item.title: E2B
item.description:
E2B gives AI agents a safe computer. When a language model writes code, running it directly on a server is risky. E2B creates an isolated sandbox in the cloud, executes the code, returns the output and files, and shuts it down. Startup is fast enough to be used inside an agent loop.

Developers use its SDKs for Python and JavaScript to start sandboxes, run commands, read and write files, and stream results. It supports data analysis agents, coding assistants, and tools that need browsers or desktops, and templates define the environment. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Fivetran
item.description:
Fivetran handles the extract and load steps of data pipelines. A team connects sources such as SaaS applications, databases, and files, picks a destination warehouse, and Fivetran keeps the data synced, adapting automatically when source schemas change. This saves engineers from building and maintaining custom connectors.

The company merged with dbt Labs, the maker of the popular transformation tool, bringing loading and transformation together under one roof. Related products include a metadata and governance layer, and tools that prepare data for AI agents. Features for monitoring, anomaly detection, and lineage help teams trust their data.

item.title: Freshdesk
item.description: Freshdesk gives support teams a single place to handle customer requests. Messages from email, a web form, live chat, phone, and channels like WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram land in a shared inbox as tickets that can be assigned, tagged, prioritized, and tracked against service-level targets. A knowledge base lets customers find answers on their own, and a customer portal shows the status of their requests. It is used by companies from small startups to large support organizations.

item.title: IBM Watson Government
item.description:
IBM Watson Government packages IBM’s AI offerings for the public sector. Agencies use them for tasks such as analyzing large volumes of text, extracting information from documents, supporting citizen service chatbots, and detecting fraud or anomalies in data. The emphasis is on meeting security and compliance standards that governments require.

The services run on IBM’s cloud and in hybrid environments, with options for on-premises deployment. Newer watsonx products add generative AI and governance tools for tracking models and risks, which agencies need under rules for responsible AI.

item.title: Jan
item.description:
Jan lets you use language models without sending data anywhere. After installing the app, you browse a model hub, download models such as Llama, Mistral, or Qwen in a size your hardware can handle, and chat with them offline. Everything runs on your machine, which is attractive to people concerned about privacy or working without internet access, and it avoids per-use fees.

It is more than a chat window. Jan can connect to remote services like OpenAI and Anthropic with your own API keys, so you can switch between local and cloud models in one interface. A local server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so other tools can use your models, and support for the Model Context Protocol lets assistants use tools. The project also develops its own small models tuned for tasks.

item.title: Lambda Labs
item.description:
Lambda started by selling deep learning workstations and servers to researchers and grew into a GPU cloud. Developers rent instances with NVIDIA GPUs, from single machines to large clusters, pre-configured with the Lambda Stack of machine learning software, so they can start training or running models quickly. Its focus on AI workloads and straightforward pricing has made it a favorite among startups, universities, and AI labs.

The company offers several ways to buy compute. On-demand instances are billed by the hour, reserved capacity provides discounted access for longer commitments, and 1-Click clusters let teams spin up multi-node setups for large training runs. Lambda also sells hardware for on-premises use, including workstations and servers, and offers inference services for deploying models.

item.title: Langflow
item.description:
Langflow makes it possible to design an AI application by connecting blocks on a canvas. Components represent language models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools, and you wire them together to define how data flows. An integrated playground lets you chat with the flow, inspect each step, and adjust it, which is useful for experimenting with retrieval and agent behavior without writing a full application.

Flows can be exported and run as API endpoints or embedded in apps, and you can write custom components in Python when the built-in ones are not enough. It works with many model providers and vector databases, and supports multi-agent setups and Model Context Protocol servers. Teams use it for prototypes, internal assistants, and RAG pipelines before moving to code.

item.title: Magento
item.description:
Magento was created as an open-source e-commerce framework and became one of the most customizable platforms for online stores. Merchants with complex needs use it to manage large catalogs, multiple storefronts and currencies, custom pricing and checkout, and integrations with ERP and other systems. A huge ecosystem of extensions, agencies, and developers supports it.

Adobe acquired Magento and sells a commercial version, Adobe Commerce, with additional features for B2B selling, merchandising, and cloud hosting and support, plus integration with Adobe’s marketing and analytics products. Adobe Sensei AI powers features such as product recommendations and search. The free Magento Open Source edition continues for those who want to host and manage their own stores.

item.title: Manus
item.description: Manus gained attention as an agent that completes whole tasks instead of answering questions. You describe a goal, such as researching a market, comparing products, building a small site, or analyzing a spreadsheet, and Manus plans the work, opens a browser, writes and runs code in its own cloud environment, and produces deliverables like reports, slides, and files. You can watch what it does and step in, and it continues running in the background.

item.title: Microsoft Government Cloud
item.description:
Azure Government is a separate cloud region set up for US federal, state, and local agencies and their partners. It runs in data centers staffed by screened US personnel and is isolated from commercial Azure, which allows it to meet compliance regimes for sensitive government data.

Agencies use it for the usual range of cloud work, including hosting applications, analytics, and AI. Services such as Azure OpenAI and Copilot have been made available in versions that meet government requirements, which lets agencies use generative AI with data protections.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate connects apps and automates repetitive work. Users build flows that trigger on events, such as an email arriving or a form submission, and perform actions in hundreds of services. It works smoothly with Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, and Dynamics.

AI features extend it. Copilot lets people describe a flow in plain language, AI Builder processes documents and forms, and agent capabilities handle more open-ended tasks. Desktop flows use robotic process automation to control applications that have no API.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate helps people automate repetitive work without code. In a visual designer, users create flows that start from a trigger, such as an email arriving or a form being submitted, and then run actions like saving attachments, updating a spreadsheet, sending approvals, or posting to Teams. It connects to hundreds of services, with deep integration with SharePoint, Outlook, Excel, and Dynamics 365, and handles scheduled and event-driven tasks.

It also covers robotic process automation. Desktop flows record and replay actions on a computer, allowing automation of legacy applications that lack APIs. AI Builder adds capabilities such as reading text from documents, classifying content, and making predictions, and Copilot can build a flow from a plain-language description. Newer features support AI agents that use flows as tools.

item.title: Modal
item.description:
Modal removes much of the setup around running compute. A developer writes Python, adds decorators that say what hardware and packages are needed, and Modal builds the container, starts it on demand, scales to many machines, and shuts it down when finished. Startup is fast, which makes it practical for bursty workloads.

Typical uses include model inference, fine-tuning, batch jobs, data processing, and running sandboxes for agents. Features such as web endpoints, scheduled jobs, volumes for storage, and notebooks cover a range of needs. Pricing is based on seconds of compute.

item.title: Ollama
item.description:
Ollama made local AI simple. You install it, run a command such as ollama run with a model name, and it downloads the model and starts a chat in your terminal. It handles the details of quantization and GPU acceleration, so models like Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, and many others run on ordinary laptops and desktops. Everything stays on your machine, so it’s private and works offline.

It is a building block for developers. Ollama exposes a local REST API, including an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so apps and tools can use your local models, and many projects such as Open WebUI, coding assistants, and agent frameworks integrate with it. Modelfiles let you customize system prompts and parameters, and recent versions add a desktop app, support for multimodal models, and optional cloud-hosted models for those too big to run locally.

item.title: Oracle SCM
item.description:
Oracle SCM Cloud brings the functions of a supply chain together in one cloud application suite. It covers planning demand and supply, buying from suppliers, managing inventory and warehouses, running manufacturing, handling orders and fulfillment, and moving goods through transportation and global trade, with product lifecycle management for design data. Because it shares data with Oracle’s finance and HR applications, companies can connect supply chain decisions to financial outcomes.

AI and analytics support the suite. Machine learning improves demand forecasts and supply plans, predictive models flag delays and quality risks, and generative AI assistants help users find information and complete tasks. Oracle has been adding AI agents that can handle routine actions across processes. The suite is delivered in the cloud and updated regularly.

item.title: Paperspace
item.description:
Paperspace rents GPU computing by the hour. Users launch virtual machines with GPUs for training models, running experiments, or heavy graphics, and connect remotely. Gradient adds managed Jupyter notebooks and workflows that make it easy to start without setting up servers.

DigitalOcean acquired Paperspace and has been integrating it with its cloud offerings, aiming to give developers and small teams access to GPUs with simple pricing. Students and independent researchers have long used it for coursework and experiments.

item.title: Penpot
item.description:
Penpot is built for collaboration between designers and developers. It uses open web standards, so designs map to real code, and supports flexible layouts based on CSS grid and flex. Teams create prototypes, design systems, and shared components in a browser.

Being open source matters to some teams. They can host Penpot themselves, keep control of their data, and avoid vendor lock-in, and developers can inspect designs and get code in a familiar form. AI features and plugins extend the tool.

item.title: Replit
item.description:
Replit began as an online code editor and runtime that supported dozens of languages with no installation. Open a browser tab, start a project, and your code runs immediately on Replit’s servers. That made it popular in schools, coding bootcamps, and with beginners, and its multiplayer editing lets several people work in the same project at once. Projects are hosted, so sharing or deploying an app takes a click.

The current focus is Replit Agent, which builds software from natural language. You describe an app, and the agent writes code, sets up the environment, installs packages, creates a database, tests the result, and deploys it. You can keep chatting to refine features or fix bugs, or open the code and edit it directly. The aim is to let people without programming experience make working apps, and to let developers move faster. A mobile app lets you build and test from a phone.

item.title: Roboflow
item.description:
Roboflow helps teams build computer vision applications without starting from scratch. You upload images or video, label objects with AI-assisted annotation tools, and Roboflow handles formatting, augmentation, and splitting data into training sets. It then trains or fine-tunes models such as YOLO and other popular architectures, and shows performance metrics so you can see where the model fails and what data to add.

Deployment is a main focus. Models can run through a hosted API, on your own servers, or at the edge on devices such as NVIDIA Jetson or a mobile phone. Workflows let you chain models with logic and actions, for example detecting a defect, counting items, and sending an alert to a system. Roboflow Universe is a public collection of datasets and pretrained models shared by the community, which gives a fast start for common tasks.

item.title: RunPod
item.description:
RunPod rents GPU computing in several forms. Users launch pods with a chosen GPU for development and training, or deploy serverless endpoints that scale with traffic for inference. Templates for common tools like Stable Diffusion and popular language model setups speed up starting.

Storage volumes persist data across sessions, and a community cloud offers lower prices on capacity from independent hosts alongside a secure cloud with data center hardware. Per-second billing suits bursty work.

item.title: Salesforce Einstein
item.description:
Einstein brought AI to Salesforce customers well before generative AI became popular. Predictive features score leads and opportunities, forecast revenue, recommend next best actions, and flag at-risk accounts, using each company’s own CRM data. Einstein Discovery finds patterns and suggests what drives outcomes, and bots and analytics features extend the same ideas to service and marketing.

With generative AI, Einstein has expanded to write emails, summarize records and cases, and generate service replies, grounded in customer data and protected by the Einstein Trust Layer, which masks sensitive information and prevents customer data from being used to train outside models. The conversational assistant evolved into Agentforce, which builds autonomous agents on the same foundation, so Einstein now refers to a mix of older predictive features and the generative AI infrastructure.

item.title: Sisense
item.description:
Sisense helps organizations analyze data and share insights. Analysts connect data sources, build models and dashboards, and users explore results in a browser. Its strength is embedding: software companies place Sisense charts and analytics inside their products for customers.
